content: Epilepsy can significantly affect the health-related quality of life (HRQOL) of individuals and their families. This has led to growing clinical interest in psychological treatments that are evidence-based and aim to improve both psychological and seizure-related outcomes for people with epilepsy. This review is an updated version of the original Cochrane Review published in 2017. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of psychological treatments on HRQOL outcomes in individuals with epilepsy. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted on August 12, 2019, without language restrictions. These databases included the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), MEDLINE, PsycINFO, PubMed, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). References from included studies and relevant reviews were also screened, and researchers in the field were contacted to identify unpublished studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs. The primary outcome was HRQOL. Psychological treatments were broadly defined to include skills-based psychological interventions and education-only interventions designed to improve HRQOL, seizure frequency and severity, and psychiatric or behavioral health comorbidities. These interventions were compared to treatment as usual (TAU), active control groups (e.g., social support groups), or antidepressant pharmacotherapy. A total of 36 completed RCTs involving 3,526 participants were included in the review. Of these, 27 studies focused on skills-based psychological interventions, while nine studies investigated education-only interventions. Six studies targeted children and adolescents, three studies included both adolescents and adults, and the remaining studies focused on adults. Data from 11 studies (643 participants) were pooled based on clinical and methodological homogeneity. These studies used the Quality of Life in Epilepsy-31 (QOLIE-31) or other QOLIE inventories (e.g., QOLIE-89, QOLIE-31-P) that could be converted to QOLIE-31 scores. The analysis revealed significant improvements in the QOLIE-31 total score and six subscales, including emotional well-being, energy and fatigue, overall quality of life, seizure worry, medication effects, and cognitive functioning. The mean improvement in the QOLIE-31 total score was 5.23 points (95% CI 3.02 to 7.44; P < 0.001), and the mean improvement in the overall quality of life score was 5.95 points (95% CI 3.05 to 8.85; P < 0.001). These changes exceeded the minimally important change (MIC) thresholds, indicating clinically meaningful improvements in HRQOL following psychological interventions. However, the certainty of the evidence was downgraded to moderate due to serious risks of bias in some of the included studies. Despite this limitation, the findings suggest that psychological treatments for adults with epilepsy may lead to meaningful improvements in overall HRQOL. The authors concluded that skills-based psychological interventions can improve HRQOL in adults and adolescents with epilepsy. Incorporating these interventions into patient-centered management may provide additional benefits. The evidence supporting these conclusions is of moderate certainty. For future research, investigators should adhere to CONSORT guidelines to improve the quality of reporting. Detailed descriptions of intervention protocols are essential to ensure reproducibility. The use of standardized HRQOL inventories, such as QOLIE-31, QOLIE-31-P, and QOLIE-89, is recommended to enhance comparability across studies. There is a notable lack of RCTs involving pediatric populations and individuals with epilepsy and intellectual disabilities, highlighting a critical gap in the literature. To improve the quality of RCT designs, researchers should ensure proper randomization with allocation concealment and blinded outcome assessment. Given the high attrition rates in studies requiring active participation, intention-to-treat analyses should be conducted. Additionally, treatment fidelity and competence should be assessed and reported, as these factors are crucial for evaluating the risk of bias.
